processing: Unopened hangbaiju buds are steamed and then baked dry. Sources differ on details, and some producers may dry the buds without steaming.
harvest_season: Late autumn, in the first passes before the flowers open. The first batch at the end of October is the most prized and sold as tai ju wang.
appearance_wet: Plump buds that stay small and whole, with little opening of the petals.
taste_profile: Fragrant and clean with a gentle sweetness, as with hangbaiju, in a more concentrated, more aromatic form than open flowers.

brewing.notes: Buds need a little longer than open flowers to give up their flavour. Refill until the cup goes thin.

vintage_note: Sold by the current autumn harvest, with the new crop from late October on. It is not aged: look for even, pale buds and a sweet smell. The first batch is marketed as tai ju wang, a label sellers use loosely.
description:
Tai ju means roughly foetal chrysanthemum, and it is just that: the unopened bud of hangbaiju, the white tea chrysanthemum of Tongxiang in Zhejiang. Same plant as the open flower, picked earlier.

Picking in the first passes, while the head is still closed, gives a tight little bud with a stronger scent. The buds are then steamed and baked, although accounts vary and other producers may treat them differently. Open hangbaiju, by comparison, is traditionally steamed and sun-dried.

In the cup it is pale, clean and gently sweet, and Chinese consumer writing rates bud pickings above full flowers for sensory quality. Give it hot water and a few minutes, since closed buds release more slowly.

When buying, look for evenly sized, compact, pale buds, and avoid dark or crumbled ones. The name tells you the stage, not the place, so tai ju may come from beyond Tongxiang. Try it next to open hangbaiju to see what the early picking changes.
history:
Little is documented about tai ju as a separate product, and it has no history apart from hangbaiju. It is a picking grade within that older Tongxiang crop, not a separate plant or a separate tradition.

The prestige of the first batch, and the name tai ju wang for it, appears in modern Chinese consumer writing and in the tea trade.
